title: What agentic workflows require of people and organisations · hancrafted
description: What an agent and an agentic workflow are, how far a person can step out of the loop for each task, the skills each person needs (plan back from the goal, agree contracts at the seams, review the result), and what the organisation must provide so the workflow is designed around the goal, not the org chart.

How far you step out (1/2) Page 1 of 2 In, on or out of the loop Three levels of human oversight, set per task: the same workflow keeps a person in for one task, on for another and out for a third. Chosen per task In the loop Human in the loop · HITL The agent acts only after a person approves. The gatekeeper approves each step On the loop Human on the loop · HOTL It acts on its own while a person watches and can step in. The pilot watches, steps in on exceptions Out of the loop Human out of the loop · HOOTL It acts without any person, who sees only the result. The auditor checks the logs afterwards One task, three ways Venue · Book a venue for 200 on 20 June Goal 20 June: everyone celebrates together and gets home safely Agent In the loop Proposes a venue Nothing is booked until you say yes. Agent On the loop Books the venue and reports You read the reports and step in if something looks wrong. Agent Out of the loop Books the venue You get the confirmation. Risk of a wrong result: highest where a person approves Speed highest where nobody waits Borrowed terms The words: military policy on weapon autonomy, 2012 The concept: supervisory control in aircraft

How far you step out (2/2) Page 2 of 2 Reviewability sets the distance A task's level is set by what a wrong result can do and by how well you can check the result; making it checkable moves it out. In, on or out of the loop Origin of the three terms the triad comes from a 2012 report on weapon autonomy: in the loop means force only with a human command, on the loop means under a human operator who can override, out of the loop means without any human input 1 . Sources (1) Human Rights Watch and Harvard IHRC, Losing Humanity (19 Nov 2012) ( opens in a new tab ) hrw.org Two senses of "on" the EU 2019 ethics guidelines define on the loop as intervening during design and monitoring operation, which differs from the military override sense used here; the guidelines have no out-of-the-loop term 1 . Sources (1) EU High-Level Expert Group on AI, Ethics Guidelines for Trustworthy AI (8 Apr 2019) ( opens in a new tab ) ec.europa.eu Approving to monitoring experienced users shift from approving individual actions to monitoring the agent and intervening when needed 1 . Sources (1) Anthropic, Measuring AI agent autonomy in practice (18 Feb 2026) ( opens in a new tab ) anthropic.com Out is a per-step property no source claims a person is out of the loop for a whole lifecycle; the humans move to specs and outcome checks 1 . Sources (1) Willison, How StrongDM's AI team build serious software without even looking at the code ( opens in a new tab ) simonwillison.net Regulation limits out for high-risk uses, EU AI Act Article 14 requires that a person can override and stop the system 1 . Sources (1) EU AI Act (Regulation 2024/1689), Article 14 Human oversight ( opens in a new tab ) artificialintelligenceact.eu Aviation supplied the concept, not the words Sheridan traces supervisory control to computers replacing direct manual control in aircraft, which left the person "in a new role of monitor and goal-constraint setter"; no source traces the words "in, on, out of the loop" to aviation, they come from the military policy above 1 . Sources (1) Sheridan, Human Supervisory Control (Handbook of Systems Engineering and Management, Wiley, 1999, ch. 16) ( opens in a new tab ) hlaszny.com Levels are not a strict ladder the FAA warns that describing automation as a linear hierarchy of levels is difficult to apply operationally, and that responsibility for flightpath management stays with the pilots at all times; it concerns airline pilots, so carrying it to agents is an analogy 1 . Sources (1) FAA, Advisory Circular 120-123, Flightpath Management (21 Nov 2022) ( opens in a new tab ) faa.gov

Reviewability sets the distance Software is easy to check "Software is unusually amenable to supervisory oversight because the outputs can be tested"; where checking needs the expertise that producing took, trust may build more slowly 1 . Sources (1) Anthropic, Measuring AI agent autonomy in practice (18 Feb 2026) ( opens in a new tab ) anthropic.com Vigilance is no check complacency and automation bias occur in naive and expert people and are not removed by training or instructions, so the check must be built into the result 1 . Sources (1) Parasuraman and Manzey, Complacency and Bias in Human Use of Automation: An Attentional Integration (Human Factors 52(3), 2010) ( opens in a new tab ) doi.org Level is a design choice the level of automation is set per function, judged by human performance consequences and the cost of errors, which is why a task may stay in for reasons other than checkability 1 . Sources (1) Parasuraman, Sheridan, Wickens, A Model for Types and Levels of Human Interaction with Automation (IEEE Trans. SMC-A 30(3), 2000) ( opens in a new tab ) doi.org Oversight follows risk in the rules the EU AI Act requires oversight measures "commensurate with the risks, level of autonomy and context of use" of a high-risk system 1 . Sources (1) EU AI Act (Regulation 2024/1689), Article 14 Human oversight ( opens in a new tab ) artificialintelligenceact.eu Risk as a tool rating OpenAI tells builders to rate each tool low, medium or high by factors such as read-only versus write access, reversibility and financial impact, and to trigger human oversight for sensitive, irreversible or high-stakes actions until confidence in the agent grows 1 . Sources (1) OpenAI, A practical guide to building agents ( opens in a new tab ) cdn.openai.com Risk is one input, not the rule no source says risk alone decides the level; the aviation-derived model ranks the effect on human performance first and the cost of errors second, so combining risk and checkability into one per-task choice is a synthesis 1 . Sources (1) Parasuraman, Sheridan, Wickens, A Model for Types and Levels of Human Interaction with Automation (IEEE Trans. SMC-A 30(3), 2000) ( opens in a new tab ) doi.org

A thought experiment 0:00 – 0:24 Imagine the board Imagine you are the manager of a summer party for 200 colleagues from five offices, and you have hired four excellent freelancers to plan it, one each for Activities, Travel, Venue and Food and drinks. They never meet and they never call each other, because the only thing they share is a board where everyone leaves notes.
What an agentic workflow is 0:00 – 0:12 Name the thing Before we fix the board, we need two terms to stand on. What is an agent, and what makes a workflow agentic? Term first, then the board.

How far you step out 0:00 – 0:18 Open question The definition left one thing open, which is how much of a person stays in the workflow. That is not one setting for the whole company, it is a choice you make for each task, and it is the next thing to learn.

In, on or out of the loop 0:00 – 0:15 In Human in the loop means the agent acts only after a person has approved. Take booking the venue for the party: the agent proposes a venue, and nothing is booked until you say yes. 0:15 – 0:31 On Human on the loop means the agent acts on its own while a person watches and can step in. Now the agent books the venue itself, you read its reports, and you step in when something looks wrong. 0:31 – 0:43 Out Human out of the loop means the agent acts without any person, who sees only the result. The agent books the venue, and all you get is the confirmation. 0:43 – 1:06 Borrowed terms These three terms were borrowed from automation outside AI, from fields where an automated action often cannot be undone, so what role the person plays was decided on purpose and not left to chance. The detail is in the Speaker notes. We borrow them because the question is the same for your agents. 1:06 – 1:17 Per task So you choose per task, not per company. Minimal intervention stops being a vague promise and becomes a setting that you choose, task by task.

Reviewability sets the distance 0:00 – 0:19 The rule You can step out of the loop only as far as you can check the result. Where checking costs as much as doing the work yourself, stepping out does not save you anything, it only means you accept a risk that nobody looks at. 0:19 – 0:37 Hypothesis, said openly The rule that you can step out only as far as you can check is my hypothesis, and I say so openly; the evidence for it comes mostly from software, so treat it as a good bet and not as a law. 0:37 – 0:51 Risk too Checkability is only half of it. What a wrong result can do also helps set the level, so the more damage a wrong result can cause, the more a person stays in. 0:51 – 1:08 Make it checkable That makes the check the lever you control. Give the activity a test it can pass, such as everyone can join, wheelchair access, no fitness needed, and the same task can move from in the loop to on the loop.

What it requires of each person 0:00 – 0:18 Skills behind the failures Let's go back to the board. Each of the four failures came from a skill that was missing in a person, and there are three skills in all. Each one has a name, and we take them one at a time.

What it requires of the organisation 0:00 – 0:12 From people to the company Skills in your people are not enough. The workflow they draw has a shape of its own, and that shape comes from the organisation they work in.
